paras: The attempted lynching of George Mitchell and Mike Stevens was an attempt by a mob, in late July 1895, to storm the jail at Live Oak, Florida, and lynch two Black men condemned for the murder of a white man, Alfred Ryberg. The attempt failed, and both men were later hanged by the state, Mitchell on August 1 and Stevens on September 18. Papers reported the mob attack in a single sentence of a dispatch that cast lynching as the expected alternative to clemency.

Ryberg, described as a white man and in one brief as "a Swede," was beaten and robbed on a freight train on which three Black train hands worked. According to the Savannah Morning News correspondent at Live Oak, Ryberg's dying statement named the three train hands, and the case against them was circumstantial but strong. Henry Brown, Mitchell and Stevens were convicted and sentenced to death.

Brown was hanged on July 17 and swore on the scaffold that he alone had killed Ryberg and that Mitchell and Stevens were innocent. A report of Brown's execution added that "there was talk of lynching Mitchell and Stevens." The Savannah correspondent wrote that the county had been "for many weeks" on the verge of a lynching because of a general belief that the executions would not take place, a belief the report tied to "frequent long delays and commutations."

A respite then followed: the Birmingham Age-Herald's copy said only Stevens was respited, while the Richmond Times said both Mitchell and Stevens were. A Live Oak special to the Jacksonville Times-Union reported on August 1 that the respite "caused such indignation that a mob attempted to storm the jail and lynch Mitchell and Stevens a few days ago." The coverage gives no date, size, leaders or details of the attempt, and does not say how it was turned back.

The governor let the law take its course with Mitchell but was still weighing Stevens' appeal for clemency. The same dispatch said Stevens would probably be allowed to hang, "as the chances are that he would be lynched if clemency were extended."

Mitchell was hanged publicly at Live Oak on August 1 before about 1,000 spectators, protesting his innocence to the end. The Savannah correspondent then wrote that there was "no further fear of a lynching," since everyone believed Stevens would soon hang. Stevens was hanged publicly on September 18, also protesting his innocence, before a small crowd that included white women holding babies.
No report of arrests or any inquiry into the attempt on the jail was found in the coverage.

The mob attempt reached print only through the Times-Union special, which the Age-Herald ran under "Died Like a Man" and which the Richmond Times, the Richmond Dispatch and the Manning Times also printed. Each treated it as one sentence in a story about the legal hanging, and the Manning Times headline, "Three Lives for One," counted the executions rather than the attempt on the jail. Shorter wire items in the Pawtucket Tribune, the San Francisco Call and the Mount Holly News reported Mitchell's hanging without mentioning the mob.

The Savannah Morning News correspondent framed lynching sentiment as a reaction to delays "that serve to defeat justice," while noting that some spectators thought Mitchell might have been innocent. No coverage of the attempt appeared in the Black press searched.

Accounts differ on the respite, which the Age-Herald gave to Stevens alone and the Richmond Times to both men. They also differ on guilt: Brown's scaffold statement cleared Mitchell and Stevens, while Stevens was said to have blamed Brown and Mitchell, and Live Oak residents reportedly believed Brown died lying.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of George Mitchell and Mike Stevens
bases: A Live Oak special said a mob attempted to storm the jail to lynch two condemned Black prisoners, Mitchell and Stevens, after a respite (A2, A3); both were later hanged legally (A2, A12).

The mob's attempt on the jail failed and neither man was killed by it; both were later executed by the state (A2, A12). The mob, of unstated size, acted against a respite for men convicted of murder (A2, A3).

The jail-storming report appears only in one Live Oak special to the Times-Union and its wire copies (A2, A3, A6, A10); a separate Live Oak report speaks only of the county being 'on the verge of a lynching' (A4), and a July report of 'talk of lynching' (A9) supports the threat but not the attack.
